issues.legal_issue: A legislature may authorize an outside authority to extend the operation of a complete enactment where the authority’s role is conditional on whether the circumstances that prompted the enactment continue.
material_facts: The enactment fixed an initial period of operation and authorized an outside authority to extend it by notification.
The enactment’s preamble identified the circumstances that prompted it, and the authority to extend its operation was conferred so that it could continue if those circumstances persisted.
issues.conclusion: The authority to extend the enactment’s operation was conditional legislation, not an invalid delegation of legislative power, and was intra vires.
issues.legal_principle: Under Queen v. Burah, legislation is conditional rather than delegated when the legislature enacts the law completely and leaves an outside authority to decide whether a condition for its operation is met. The Court relied on In re The Delhi Laws Act, 1912 and State of Bombay v. Narothamdas Jethabai, and dissented from Jatindra Nath Gupta v. The State of Bihar insofar as it held that an outside authority could not be given power to extend an enactment’s life.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enabling_law: A party in a constitutional challenge contends that a law improperly gives an outside authority power over its continued operation.
predicates.law_complete_when_enacted: The legislature enacted the law in complete form and fixed its initial period of operation.
predicates.outside_authority_only_decides_continuat: An outside authority was empowered only to decide whether the already-enacted law should continue to operate.
predicates.continuation_depends_on_persisting_condi: The authority’s decision to continue the law depended on whether the circumstances prompting it persisted.

issues.definition: When a complete law may continue only if an outside authority finds that the circumstances prompting it persist, the authority to extend the law is valid.

issues.legal_issue: An official may validly issue a notification under an existing statutory power even after the official’s separate legislative authority has ended.
material_facts: The notification extending the enactment’s operation was issued after the state legislature had been constituted.
The power to issue the notification had been conferred by the still-operative enactment, and the official acted under that power rather than as the state’s legislative authority.
issues.conclusion: The notification was valid because it was issued under the existing enactment, not by exercising legislative authority that had ended.
issues.legal_principle: The notification was an exercise of a power conferred by the enactment and was referable to that enactment, not to the official’s former legislative competence under Article 385 of the Constitution. Its validity therefore depended on the validity and continued operation of the enactment.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_official_not: A party in a constitutional challenge contests an official notification issued under an enactment.
predicates.enabling_law_remained_in_force: The enactment conferring the notification power remained in force when the notification was issued.
predicates.official_exercised_preexisting_statutory: The official issued the notification under a power previously conferred by the enactment.
predicates.official_did_not_make_new_law: The official acted under the enactment rather than exercising legislative authority to create new law.

issues.definition: A notification is valid when the enabling law remains in force and the official exercises an existing statutory power rather than making new law.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature’s selection of an effective date for a protective law does not, by itself, make the resulting difference in treatment unconstitutional.
material_facts: The enactment protected tenants against ejectment or dispossession and extended a reinstatement right to tenants in occupation on a specified earlier date.
The preamble identified a growing tendency to eject tenants as the reason for providing protection.
The petitioners argued that landlords whose tenants fell outside the specified date were not subject to the same restrictions.
issues.conclusion: The date-based distinction did not make the enactment invalid under Article 14; selecting the date from which the protection operated was for the legislature to determine.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the legislature could determine the date from which a protective law would operate and that the propriety of that determination was not open to challenge in court merely because it distinguished between landlords. The stated policy and purpose of protecting tenants informed the law’s coverage.

rule.if: constitutional_equality_challenge and law_protects_a_group and legislature_identified_a_need_for_protection and legislature_selected_a_coverage_date

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge: A party contends that a law’s classification or coverage violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.law_protects_a_group: The law provides protection to a group facing a stated hardship or risk.
predicates.legislature_identified_a_need_for_protec: The legislature identified a problem that the law was intended to address.
predicates.legislature_selected_a_coverage_date: The legislature chose a date from which the law’s protection would apply, producing different treatment for people outside that coverage.

issues.definition: A coverage-date distinction is not unconstitutional merely because it treats people outside the protected group differently when the legislature identified a need for protection and selected the date of coverage.

issues.legal_issue: An exemption power is not unguided for equality purposes when the enactment’s preamble states a policy that governs the exercise of that power.
material_facts: The enactment authorized the government to exempt any person or class of persons from its operation without stating exemption criteria in that provision.
The preamble stated that the enactment was intended to protect tenants from ejectment or dispossession and to grant them relief.
issues.conclusion: The exemption power was not unguided because the preamble sufficiently stated the legislative policy governing it, so the enactment was not invalid under Article 14 on this ground.
issues.legal_principle: A preamble may supply the policy guiding an exemption power and prevent the exercise of that power from being unguided. The Court relied on Harishankar Bagla v. The State of Madhya Pradesh. It also observed that even if the exemption provision were invalid, it was severable from the rest of the enactment.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge: A party contends that an exemption power violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.exemption_power_has_no_express_criteria: The provision granting exemption power does not itself state the criteria for exercising that power.
predicates.enactment_preamble_states_governing_poli: The enactment’s preamble states a policy that governs the purpose and exercise of the exemption power.

issues.definition: An exemption power without criteria in its own provision is not unguided when the enactment’s preamble states the policy governing its exercise.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary law securing some tenure for tenants who cultivate land is not unreasonable merely because it limits a landowner’s ability to evict them.
material_facts: The enactment prevented tenants from being ejected or dispossessed without sufficient cause.
The stated purpose was to prevent landholders who had inducted tenants from getting rid of them, not to prevent owners from cultivating their own land.
The enactment was temporary emergency legislation and sought to assure actual tillers of the soil some fixity of tenure.
issues.conclusion: The enactment did not violate Article 19(1)(f) merely by restricting the landowner’s ability to evict a tenant; the restriction was not shown to be unreasonable.
issues.legal_principle: A law securing some fixity of tenure for an actual tiller is not unreasonable merely because it limits an owner’s ability to evict a tenant whom the owner inducted. The Court relied on Block v. Hirsh and treated the temporary emergency character of the law as relevant to reasonableness, citing Dr. N. B. Khare v. The State of Delhi.

predicates.constitutional_property_right_challenge: A party in a constitutional challenge contends that a law unreasonably restricts property rights.
predicates.law_secures_tenure_for_actual_cultivator: The law gives tenants who cultivate land some security of tenure.
predicates.restriction_targets_eviction_not_owner_s: The law limits eviction of an inducted tenant rather than preventing the owner from cultivating the land personally.
predicates.measure_is_temporary_emergency_legislati: The challenged restriction is part of temporary emergency legislation.

issues.definition: A temporary emergency measure securing tenure for actual cultivators is not unreasonable on this ground when it restricts eviction rather than the owner’s personal cultivation.
